overview: This three-page Department of State “List of Papers” is an archival index—rather than the underlying correspondence—to reports, telegrams, memoranda, notes, and press material concerning the sale, purchase, charter, registry, and scrapping of vessels connected with Japan’s merchant marine, chiefly from about 1931 through 1939. Its entries trace Japanese acquisitions of Canadian, British, Norwegian, and American ships; proposed registry transfers from China to Panama; and U.S. government deliberations over approving sales to Japanese interests. Particular attention is given to Yamashita Kisen’s proposed purchase of ten Lykes Brothers vessels and to whether ships sold on condition of scrapping—including Tashmoo, Fort Armstrong, and Buffalo Bridge—remained in operation.

subfiles.title: Department of State list of papers on vessel transactions for the Japanese merchant marine
subfiles.about: A three-page index summarizes papers concerning foreign vessels sold or proposed for sale to Japanese interests and associated questions of registry, scrapping, and U.S. policy.
subfiles.summary: The list indexes papers numbered 3 through 18, plus several related or unnumbered communications, covering roughly 1931–1939. Early entries concern ships acquired from Holland-America Line, Canadian National Steamers, British sources, and Norwegian whaling interests; later entries address transfers among Chinese, Panamanian, Japanese, and American registries. Much of the final portion documents Yamashita Kisen’s proposed purchase of ten vessels from Lykes Brothers and the State Department’s reluctance to support the transaction. It also records concern that Tashmoo, Fort Armstrong, and Buffalo Bridge—renamed Takusei Maru, Takuen Maru, and Kosei Maru—were still operating despite scrapping conditions attached to their sale.

interest: The list is useful as a compact roadmap to a larger documentary trail that is not itself reproduced here, preserving document numbers, dates, senders, cross-references, and summaries of otherwise dispersed records. It shows how ostensibly commercial ship sales became questions of strategic policy, registry manipulation, enforcement, and government approval during the deterioration of U.S.–Japanese relations in the late 1930s. The entries concerning vessels sold on the condition that they be scrapped—but reportedly retained in operation under Japanese names—are especially valuable for tracing both individual ship histories and possible failures of regulatory enforcement.
